lead: Pulse code modulation (PCM) sends each quantized sample as a fixed-length binary code word. The message is filtered, sampled, rounded to one of L levels and written as n bits, so the bit rate is R<sub>b</sub> = n f<sub>s</sub>: telephone speech at 8 kHz and 8 bits gives 64 kbit/s. Because the channel carries only 0s and 1s, repeaters can regenerate clean pulses, and noise does not pile up along the route. PCM is the base of digital telephony and of every audio file format.
prereq: You need: sampling and aliasing and quantization and companding.

sections.h3: The PCM chain and its bit rate

items: An anti-aliasing lowpass filter limits m(t) to f<sub>m</sub>.
A sampler takes values at f<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2f<sub>m</sub>.
A quantizer rounds each sample to one of L = 2ⁿ levels (uniform, or companded for speech).
An encoder writes the level number as an n-bit code word and sends the bits, each lasting Tb = 1/Rb.
Regenerative repeaters along the line decide each bit and send it on as a fresh pulse.
The receiver decodes each word back to its level, and a reconstruction lowpass filter smooths the steps into m(t).

blocks.text: R<sub>b</sub> in bit/s, n bits per sample, f<sub>s</sub> in samples/s, T<sub>b</sub> in seconds.

The figure traces three bits through the chain: a 1 kHz tone of peak 3.5 V sampled at 8 kHz, a 3-bit quantizer over ±4 V (Δ = 1 V, levels ±0.5, ±1.5, ±2.5, ±3.5 V) and natural binary codes 000 for −3.5 V up to 111 for +3.5 V. Some syllabi add a Gray code, in which neighbouring levels differ in one bit, so a single bit error moves the sample by only one step.

sections.h3: Bandwidth and the SNR that n buys

blocks.text: Two bandwidth figures are easy to mix. With ideal Nyquist pulses and no intersymbol interference, the minimum baseband bandwidth is B<sub>min</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2 = n f<sub>s</sub>/2; at the Nyquist rate this is n f<sub>m</sub>, so PCM needs n times the message bandwidth. Rectangular NRZ pulses have their first spectral null at R<sub>b</sub>, so their main lobe needs R<sub>b</sub>. For 64 kbit/s speech: 32 kHz minimum, 64 kHz to the first null.

Each extra bit doubles L and adds 6.02 dB of SQNR, but also adds f<sub>s</sub> bit/s of rate and f<sub>s</sub>/2 Hz of bandwidth. So SQNR in dB grows linearly with bandwidth, an exponential trade of bandwidth for SNR that analog FM cannot match. To meet a target, solve 6.02n + 1.76 ≥ SQNR for the smallest whole n.

A regenerative repeater equalizes the pulse, recovers the clock, decides 0 or 1 and sends a fresh pulse. Noise picked up on one span is discarded instead of amplified, so a long line behaves like its worst span. A wrong decision is a bit error and travels on; regeneration is not error correction.

A bit error moves the decoded sample to a wrong level, and an error in the most significant bit moves it by half the range: a click. For a uniformly distributed signal and natural binary code, the output SNR including bit errors with probability P<sub>e</sub> is
L = 2ⁿ. With no errors it is L² (the SQNR of a uniform signal, 6.02n dB); the error term takes over once 4L²P<sub>e</sub> nears 1.

This sharp fall is the PCM threshold: above about Pe = 10⁻⁶ the link is quantization-limited, below it error-limited. Since Pe falls very fast with received SNR, a few dB more signal moves a link from noisy to perfect.

examples.question: Telephone speech bandlimited to 3.4 kHz is sampled at 8 kHz with 8-bit PCM. Find the bit rate, the bit duration, the ideal minimum bandwidth, the NRZ first-null bandwidth, L and the SQNR for a full-scale sine.
steps: Nyquist rate = 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 kHz < 8 kHz, so there is no aliasing (guard band 1.2 kHz).
R<sub>b</sub> = n f<sub>s</sub> = 8 × 8000 = 64 000 bit/s; T<sub>b</sub> = 1/64 000 s = 15.6 µs.
B<sub>min</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2 = 32 kHz; NRZ first null at R<sub>b</sub> = 64 kHz.
examples.answer: 64 kbit/s, T<sub>b</sub> = 15.6 µs, 32 kHz minimum (64 kHz to the NRZ null), 256 levels, 49.9 dB.

examples.question: Encode x(t) = 3.5 sin(2π·1000t) V with the 3-bit quantizer of the figure (±4 V, Δ = 1 V, natural binary), sampling at 8 kHz at the instants t = (k + ½)T<sub>s</sub>, k = 0 to 7. Give the bit stream, the largest error and the bit rate.
steps: The phase at the samples is 2π·1000·(k + ½)/8000 = π/8 + kπ/4, so x = 3.5 sin(22.5°) = 1.339 V, 3.5 sin(67.5°) = 3.234 V, and so on.
Round to the nearest of the eight levels and read off the code: level −3.5 V is 000, −1.5 V is 010, +1.5 V is 101, +3.5 V is 111.
All errors are within ±Δ/2 = ±0.5 V; the largest is 0.266 V.
R<sub>b</sub> = 3 × 8000 = 24 kbit/s; one period (1 ms) carries 24 bits.
examples.answer: Bits 101 111 111 101 010 000 000 010; largest error 0.266 V; R<sub>b</sub> = 24 kbit/s.

traps: 64 kbit/s is a bit rate. The ideal minimum bandwidth is 32 kHz, and NRZ needs 64 kHz to its first null; 8 kHz is the sampling rate.
L = 2ⁿ, not 2n: 8 bits give 256 levels, not 16.
Regeneration removes noise, not bit errors; a wrong decision passes through every later repeater.
More bits cannot undo aliasing; that is fixed only by the filter and f<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the PCM bit-rate formula and define each symbol.
quiz.a: R<sub>b</sub> = n f<sub>s</sub>: R<sub>b</sub> in bit/s, n bits per sample, f<sub>s</sub> samples per second.

quiz.q: A 4 kHz signal is sampled at 10 kHz with 6 bits. Find R<sub>b</sub> and the ideal minimum bandwidth.
Audio bandlimited to 15 kHz is sampled 20 % above the Nyquist rate and needs SQNR ≥ 55 dB for a full-scale sine. Find n, f<sub>s</sub>, R<sub>b</sub> and B<sub>min</sub>.
quiz.a: 6.02n + 1.76 ≥ 55 gives n ≥ 8.84, so n = 9 (55.9 dB). f<sub>s</sub> = 1.2 × 30 = 36 kHz; R<sub>b</sub> = 9 × 36 000 = 324 kbit/s; B<sub>min</sub> = 162 kHz.

quiz.q: What do regenerative repeaters improve, and what can they not remove?
quiz.a: Each decides every bit and sends a fresh pulse, so noise does not add up span after span. A bit decided wrongly stays wrong and is passed on.

quiz.q: An 8-bit PCM link has P<sub>e</sub> = 10⁻⁴. Find (S/N)<sub>o</sub> and say which noise dominates.
quiz.a: L² = 65 536; 4L²P<sub>e</sub> = 26.2; (S/N)<sub>o</sub> = 65 536/27.2 = 2408, or 33.8 dB. Bit errors dominate: without them it would be 48.2 dB.

quiz.q: Why does PCM trade bandwidth for SNR better than analog modulation?
quiz.a: Each extra bit adds 6 dB of SQNR for f<sub>s</sub>/2 more bandwidth, so SNR in dB grows linearly with bandwidth (SNR grows exponentially). In wideband FM, SNR grows only with the square of the deviation ratio.

beyond: Not for the exam. CD audio is 16-bit PCM at 44.1 kHz; studio audio uses 24 bits at 96 kHz. Sigma-delta converters reach those resolutions with a 1-bit quantizer and heavy oversampling. Search next for G.711, sigma-delta ADCs and dither.
